cf.title: Logging plan of the currently running query

input.subject: Re: RFC: Logging plan of the running query

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal or the node-wrapping design, which Robert Haas accepted in the thread. The remaining points are fixable. maintenance-fit-2 asks for overhead numbers that reviewers requested and the thread never shows. standards-compat-1, maintenance-fit-1 and replication-ondisk-1 concern the 0002 request-ID patch, which no reviewer has answered yet.

brief.title: pg_log_query_plan(): log the plan of a query running in another backend
brief.problem: A DBA cannot see the plan of a long-running query until it finishes, and production systems usually do not allow a debugger. The patch targets people investigating slow queries in production.
brief.proposed_design: pg_log_query_plan(pid) sends a signal to a client backend. At the next CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS the target re-arms ExecProcNodeFirst on every node of its current plan tree, and the first node entered then writes a plain EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE) of the innermost running query to the server log. A v61-0002 patch adds request IDs kept in shared memory per backend slot, returned to the caller and printed in the log line.
user_visible_surface: SQL function pg_log_query_plan(pid integer), superuser-only by default and grantable; returns boolean in 0001 and a request ID in 0002
New LOG_SERVER_ONLY messages that carry the query text, queryid, plan, and in 0002 the request ID
New ExplainState field es->running, new explain_running.c, and an exported ExplainStringAssemble() that auto_explain also uses
New injection point log-query-interrupt and a TAP test, 014_pg_log_query_plan.pl
author_claims: Users need to see plans of long-running production queries without waiting for them to finish or using a debugger.
Logging from a node entry point is safe, while running EXPLAIN directly inside the interrupt handler is not.
Backends that never receive the request pay almost no cost, because the extra check only runs after the interrupt arrives.
Repeated calls every 0.1s during make installcheck caused no crashes, and the TAP test passed 300 runs.
The scope is kept narrow on purpose, and progress tracking, EXPLAIN options and ANALYZE are left to later patches.
brief.thread_state: Robert Haas and Andrei Lepikhov are the active reviewers, and Haas has accepted the node-wrapping design. The last message posts v61 with the request-ID 0002 patch and asks for opinions, and no reply is visible.
unclear: The thread has no measured overhead numbers for normal or targeted backends, though reviewers asked for time and memory benchmarks.
No reviewer has said whether the request-ID shared memory and the changed return type in 0002 are acceptable.
The thread does not say what happens when a parallel worker is the target, beyond an error that it is not a client backend.
No one has confirmed that clearing LogQueryPlanPending at the end of ExecutorRun handles cursors and the extended query protocol.
The thread does not say whether pg_log_backend_memory_contexts() will be aligned on PID in messages and privilege comments.

prior_attempts.title: interrogate other backends for plans of the queries they are running
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 also asked another backend for the plan of its running query, but the corpus records no reason for its return. This proposal logs from the next node entry after CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS, a design the reviewers in this thread accepted.

prior_attempts.title: Allow auto_explain to log plans before queries are executed
prior_attempts.quote: There was some discussion but no clear consensus on what should really be done.
prior_attempts.reason: Reviewers discussed the behavior but did not agree on a design. Julien Rouhaud said the final plan is still needed when log_analyze, log_buffers or log_timing are on, and suggested a cost threshold for logging before execution. The thread moved to Waiting on Author, made no further progress, and was returned with feedback.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 added an auto_explain option that logged every plan before execution and stalled on its interaction with ANALYZE-style options. This proposal works on demand for one backend, uses default EXPLAIN options and adds no GUC.

objections.title: No overhead numbers for the per-query bookkeeping every backend pays
objections.failure_scenario: An OLTP site running short pgbench-style queries upgrades. Every ExecutorRun now saves and restores a QueryDesc pointer in TransactionStateData and clears LogQueryPlanPending, and every node's first call passes an extra test. Any regression shows up only after release.
objections.argument: The claim of near-zero cost covers only the interrupt-armed path (message #118). The queryDesc save and restore in standard_ExecutorRun and the abort-time resets run for all queries (messages #152, #159). Reviewers asked for time and memory benchmarks in messages #1 and #129, and the author agreed in message #139. The thread shows no numbers.
objections.author_must_show: What do pgbench -S and a nested PL/pgSQL workload measure with and without 0001, with the feature never invoked?

critic.reasoning: The added work per ExecutorRun is small, but it runs for every query, and reviewers asked for numbers in messages #1 and #129. The author agreed in message #139 and the thread shows no measurement.

objections.title: Return type differs between 0001 and 0002, and from sibling pg_log_* functions
objections.failure_scenario: 0001 is committed for one release with a boolean result, and 0002 lands in a later release with an integer result. A monitoring script that runs `select ... where pg_log_query_plan(pid)` then fails after upgrade with a type error. A tool that treats pg_log_* functions alike also has to special-case this one.
objections.argument: The brief says 0001 returns boolean and 0002 returns a request ID. Message #197 posts them as separately reviewable steps. pg_log_backend_memory_contexts() and the pg_cancel_backend() family return boolean and report failure as false plus a WARNING, as message #138 shows. The proposal does not say what 0002 returns when the target is not a client backend, and no reviewer has accepted the new return type.
objections.author_must_show: Will 0001 and 0002 be committed together so the return type is set once, and what does 0002 return when no request is queued?

critic.reasoning: v61 posts 0002 as a separately reviewable step that changes the result from boolean to a request ID, and no reviewer has accepted that. The thread does not say what 0002 returns when the target is not a client backend.

objections.title: Request-ID shared memory in 0002 sets a protocol no reviewer has accepted
objections.failure_scenario: Two monitoring tools call pg_log_query_plan() for the same PID within a few milliseconds, and the target has only one request slot. One request ID is overwritten or rejected, so that tool waits for a log line that never appears. Users find out when the automation built on the ID stalls.
objections.argument: Message #197 adds one shared-memory slot per backend slot and a cluster-wide counter. It also changes the return type from boolean to a request ID. The author presents the slot as the future carrier for EXPLAIN options (messages #196, #197), so the layout and return type become a long-term commitment. No reviewer has replied to v61, and pg_log_backend_memory_contexts() still returns boolean, so the two sibling functions would differ.
objections.author_must_show: What happens when two callers target the same backend before it serves the first request, and why is a per-backend slot the right shape for later options?

critic.reasoning: Message #197 describes one request slot per backend slot, with a state and a spinlock, but does not say what a second caller gets while a request is pending. No reviewer has replied to v61, so the question is open.

objections.title: Request IDs restart after a server restart and repeat in the log
objections.failure_scenario: A monitoring tool calls pg_log_query_plan() and gets ID 3, then scans the server log for "request ID 3". The server restarted earlier that day, and the same log file holds an older entry with ID 3. The tool picks the wrong plan and nothing tells it so.
objections.argument: Message #197 says 0002 creates request IDs from a cluster-wide counter in shared memory. Shared memory is reset at startup and after crash recovery, so the counter starts again from the beginning while the log files are kept. Each hot standby also has its own counter, so a central log collector sees the same ID from several nodes. Matching each call to its log record was the stated purpose of 0002 (messages #193 to #195), and that matching is unreliable unless the ID is unique.
objections.author_must_show: How does an automation tool match a returned request ID to exactly one log record across restarts, crash recovery and standbys?

critic.reasoning: Message #197 keeps the counter in shared memory allocated at server startup, so IDs repeat after a restart, and the proposal does not state their scope. The log line also carries the PID, so a documented scope may be enough; the standby point adds little.

refuted.title: Request ID and queryid in the log do not uniquely identify a request
refuted.failure_scenario: An automation tool stores the returned request ID and later searches the log for it. The cluster-wide counter lives in shared memory, so after a restart it reuses IDs and the tool matches an older plan. With compute_query_id off, the message prints "queryid 0" and cannot be joined to pg_stat_activity.
refuted.argument: Message #193 justifies 0002 by tool-driven matching of a call to its log record. Message #197 describes a counter in shared memory, so it presumably restarts at server start, and the proposal does not say that IDs are unique only within one server lifetime. The log line in message #191 shows queryid 0, so the queryid part of the contract depends on a separate setting. The doc text should state these limits, or the design should avoid them.
refuted.author_must_show: Within what scope is a request ID unique, and how should a tool match a log record when IDs repeat after restart or queryid is 0?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1 for the repeated request IDs. The queryid 0 part matches existing practice: auto_explain and log_line_prefix also show no query ID when compute_query_id is off.

refuted.title: Return type of pg_log_query_plan() changes between 0001 and 0002
refuted.failure_scenario: 0001 ships in one release with pg_log_query_plan(pid) returning boolean. 0002 lands in the next release and the function returns a request ID instead. Scripts that use the result as a boolean, for example in where pg_log_query_plan(pid), fail after pg_upgrade, and users find out when their monitoring breaks.
refuted.argument: Message #196 says the request ID work is meant to be reviewed separately and placed in 0002, while 0001 stays unchanged. The pg_proc signature is a user-visible contract, and changing the return type after a release breaks existing callers. Message #196 also expects the 0002 channel to carry EXPLAIN options later, which could change the signature again. No reviewer has answered whether 0002 and its changed return type are acceptable.
refuted.author_must_show: Will 0001 and 0002 be committed together so that the SQL signature is fixed once, and if they are not, what does 0001 return that 0002 can keep?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which covers the same return type change and also asks what 0002 returns on failure.

refuted.title: A third copy of EXPLAIN option handling to keep in sync
refuted.failure_scenario: A later release adds a new EXPLAIN option or changes how ExplainStringAssemble() behaves for auto_explain. Nobody updates explain_running.c or the planned 0003 option passing, and nothing fails loudly. The logged plans quietly differ from what EXPLAIN shows.
refuted.argument: Message #134 already notes that auto_explain's option handling has drifted from ExplainOnePlan(). The patch exports ExplainStringAssemble() for both callers and adds es->running as a special case. Message #196 plans to pass EXPLAIN options through the 0002 shared-memory slot, which is a third place that must track new options.
refuted.author_must_show: How will a new EXPLAIN option reach explain_running.c and the request slot without a hand-maintained list?

critic.reasoning: Since v56 the patch uses the NewExplainState() defaults and shares ExplainStringAssemble() with auto_explain, so it adds no new option list. The drift is in existing auto_explain code, which message #134 says is not this patch's fault, and 0003 is not yet proposed.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a pg_proc entry for pg_log_query_plan(), and 0002 changes its return type.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds the ExplainState field es->running and exports ExplainStringAssemble(), which auto_explain also uses.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Return type differs between 0001 and 0002, and from sibling pg_log_* functions

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The function is superuser-only by default and grantable, and it writes query text and plans of other sessions to the server log.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Return type differs between 0001 and 0002, and from sibling pg_log_* functions

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds explain_running.c, re-arming of ExecProcNodeFirst on every plan node, and in 0002 shared-memory request slots.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Every ExecutorRun saves and restores a QueryDesc pointer and clears LogQueryPlanPending, even when nobody calls the function.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: What do pgbench -S and a nested PL/pgSQL workload measure with and without 0001 when pg_log_query_plan() is never called?
Will 0001 and 0002 be committed together so the return type is set once, and what does 0002 return when the target is not a client backend?
What does a second caller get when it targets a backend whose request slot still holds an unserved request?
Within what scope is a request ID unique, and how does a tool match one log record after a server restart resets the counter?
Does clearing LogQueryPlanPending at the end of ExecutorRun work for cursors and the extended query protocol, where one query spans several ExecutorRun calls?

committability.owner_note: The owner must know executor node dispatch and interrupt handling. Robert Haas reviews in the thread and accepted the node-wrapping design.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the re-arming of ExecProcNodeFirst across all plan node types and for the per-query QueryDesc tracking, for as long as the executor keeps this shape. With 0002, the owner also signs for the shared-memory request slots and the return type.
committability.author_follow_up: The author has kept the entry alive through 11 CommitFests, rebased it repeatedly and posted v61, which suggests the author stays for fixes.

priority.reason: DBAs who investigate slow queries in production have asked for this since 2021, and a committer accepted the core design. The patch touches the executor, procsignal and EXPLAIN code, so review needs care, and 0002 still needs a first answer.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check that re-arming ExecProcNodeFirst is safe for every node type and for cursors. It also could not check how the 0002 request slot behaves under concurrent callers.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow auto_explain to log plans before queries are executed
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an auto_explain option, log_before_query, that logs every plan before the query runs, so the plan of a query that gets stuck is still logged. With the option on, only the duration is logged after execution.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers discussed the behavior but did not agree on a design. Julien Rouhaud said the final plan is still needed when log_analyze, log_buffers or log_timing are on, and suggested a cost threshold for logging before execution. The thread moved to Waiting on Author, made no further progress, and was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There was some discussion but no clear consensus on what should really
be done.

precedents_retrieved.title: Exclude partition constaint checking in query execution plan for partitioned table queries
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the planner remove restriction clauses from scans of partitions or inheritance children when those clauses are already implied by the partition or CHECK constraints, to avoid redundant filter evaluation. Earlier versions also extended operator_predicate_proof (first with hard-coded integer operators, later with a range-type lookup) so that, for example, k < 20001 could prove k <= 20000.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback because the latest reviews had not been addressed. David Rowley rejected the range-type approach to predicate proof, for performance, collation and pg_range scan reasons, and asked that the predicate_implied_by() changes become a separate patch. He also asked for new benchmarks on planning overhead. His last review raised a concern that removing quals could prevent an index such as (a,b) from being used. Andres Freund raised an earlier concern about planning overhead, but his message is not shown.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The latest reviews have not been addressed yet, so I have marked
this as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: query logging of prepared statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch stops repeating the prepared statement text in the log on every bind and execute, for both SQL EXECUTE and protocol-level PQexecPrepared, to cut log volume. Later versions log the text at Parse instead and, following a suggestion from Alvaro Herrera, use a flag in the portal so the statement is logged once.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Alvaro Herrera found that v2 dropped the statement text for unnamed statements under log_statement=all, so the patch needed more work. Andres Freund then objected to logging the statement only once: with long-running connections and many executions of one prepared statement, the query text would be far back in the log file or in an earlier rotated file. The author said he would tentatively withdraw the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I'm sympathetic to the desire to reduce log volume, but I'm fearful this would make log analysis much harder.

precedents_retrieved.title: More stable query plans via more predictable column statistics
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes compute_scalar_stats() in ANALYZE so the MCV cut-off ignores NULLs in the sample and recomputes the histogram bin count inside the MCV loop. The goal is to stop common values from showing up as duplicates in histogram_bounds, so statistics and plans stay more stable between ANALYZE runs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra's review accepted the NULL handling as a bug fix but said the rest is a change of MCV cut-off policy. Longer MCV lists make estimation and planning more expensive, and the analysis covered only ANALYZE, not the estimation side. He also found the new loop, with its falling threshold, hard to reason about, and noted that the ndistinct estimator has the same NULL problem. The author agreed these points needed more work, and the entry was returned with feedback about a week later.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Overall, I think this is really about deciding when to cut-off the MCV, so that it does not grow needlessly large - as Robert pointed out, the larger the list, the more expensive the estimation (and thus planning).

precedents_retrieved.title: File content logging during execution of COPY queries
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andrew Dunstan, Tom Lane, Stephen Frost
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch proposed logging the data rows read or written by COPY ... FROM and COPY ... TO when log_statement='all', so that workloads using COPY could be fully recorded for replay and benchmarking. After objections it was revised to add a separate boolean parameter, log_copy, to control this.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andrew Dunstan and Tom Lane objected that log_statement is meant for logging statements, not data, and that the change would repeat potentially gigabytes of COPY data into the server log. Stephen Frost questioned logging COPY TO data at all, since results of SELECT and RETURNING are not logged, so network capture would still be needed to record all data. The patch's assigned reviewer was reminded to respond, and the commitfest manager then closed the entry as rejected, noting that some people were against the approach.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It sounds good when you're looking at toy examples,
but not when it means repeating gigabytes of COPY data into the log.

precedents_retrieved.title: CLUSTER command progress monitor
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_stat_progress_cluster view that reports the phase of CLUSTER and VACUUM FULL, the scan method, and counts of heap tuples scanned. Phases cover heap scan, sort, writing the new heap, file swap, index rebuild and final cleanup, with a combined phase for the index-scan path.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas objected that the design reports only the phase name for sorting and for the index-scan path, though scanning and writing the new heap take most of the runtime. He also asked to drop heap_tuples_total, which only copies reltuples. The author agreed to rework it, including a sort progress counter, but no new version came before the commitfest closed, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I would guess that scanning the
heap and writing the new heap would ordinarily account for most of the
runtime, or at least enough that you're going to want something more
than just knowing that's the phase you're in.

precedents_retrieved.title: VACUUM Progress Checker
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a way to report the progress of long-running VACUUM commands, such as pages scanned and the current phase, so DBAs can judge whether to wait or abort. The design moved from a shared-preload-library hook to a general per-backend progress-reporting facility in PgBackendStatus, with counter and message update functions, exposed through a pg_stat_vacuum_progress view.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch was still being actively reworked when the commitfest closed, so it was returned with feedback and the author was asked to resubmit to the next commitfest. The reporting interface and its counters were not yet settled: reviewers were still asking for a lightweight API that updates a single counter or message, for reporting the current block number, and for finer-grained index-phase reporting, and new review comments arrived on the latest version. In the previous commitfest it had already been returned as not committable, with Michael Paquier questioning the design of the progress facility.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since things are clearly still moving here, I closed it as
returned-with-feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: ANALYZE command progress checker
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_stat_progress_analyze view that reports the phase of a running ANALYZE and counters for blocks and sample rows, using the progress reporting framework that VACUUM uses. Later versions add phases for inherited sample rows and statistics computation, and a child_relid column.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas proposed moving the patch to v11 because it arrived one day before the last CommitFest, the design was not right, and the right design was still unknown. Reviewers found that the reported phases did not match where ANALYZE spends its time, and that counters reset for each child table, so inheritance trees showed wrong progress. Sample-row and block counts were also not reliable, and FDWs had no way to report progress.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It was
submitted one day before the start of the last CommitFest, the design
wasn't really right, and it's not clear even now that we know what the
right design is.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Distinguish printf-like functions that support %m from those that don't."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Distinguish printf-like functions that support %m from those that don't."
Reverted commit(s): Distinguish printf-like functions that support %m from those that don't.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 3a60c8ff892a8242b907f44702bfd9f1ff877d45.  Buildfarm
results show that that caused a whole bunch of new warnings on platforms
where gcc believes the local printf to be non-POSIX-compliant.  This
problem outweighs the hypothetical-anyway possibility of getting warnings
for misuse of %m.  We could use gnu_printf archetype when we've substituted
src/port/snprintf.c, but that brings us right back to the problem of not
getting warnings for %m.

A possible answer is to attack it in the other direction by insisting
that %m support be included in printf's feature set, but that will take
more investigation.  In the meantime, revert the previous change, and
update the comment for PGAC_C_PRINTF_ARCHETYPE to more fully explain
what's going on.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert my bad decision of about a year ago to make PortalDefineQuery responsible for copying the query string into the new Portal.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert my bad decision of about a year ago to make PortalDefineQuery responsible for copying the query string into the new Portal.  Such copying is unnecessary in the common code path through exec_simple_query, and in this case it can be enormously expensive because the string might contain a large number of individual commands; we were copying the entire, long string for each command, resulting in O(N^2) behavior for N commands. (This is the cause of bug #4079.)  A second problem with it is that PortalDefineQuery really can't risk error, because if it elog's before having set up the Portal, we will leak the plancache refcount that the caller is trying to hand off to the portal.  So go back to the design in which the caller is responsible for making sure everything is copied into the portal if necessary.

Extend comments on signal handling and cross-reference comments on signal handling functions
Threads: [PATCH] Cross-reference comments on signal handling logic

roaster_notes.note: No precedent reason applies. P1 has no recorded reason. P2 stalled on design choices for an auto_explain option, which this proposal does not use. The earlier designs abandoned inside this thread are settled: shm_mq messaging (messages #1, #3), EXPLAIN inside the interrupt handler (message #146), and the need for prior configuration (messages #131, #142).
Other contract points were settled in the thread: the PID in the message stays for consistency (#158), the function name was kept (#176), and EXPLAIN options use the defaults (#174).
The proposal adds no on-disk format, WAL record or wire protocol change. Its shared state is limited to the 0002 shared-memory request slots and the new pg_proc entry.

No security objection that would survive review. pg_log_query_plan() is superuser-only by default and needs an explicit GRANT, and output goes only to the server log at LOG_SERVER_ONLY. Message #173 and message #174 tied the default to who can read the log. That keeps the plan, query text and queryid visible only to roles that can already read the log. A grantee cannot read other users' plans through the function itself. Repeated calls only fill the log and burn CPU in the target backend, and the superuser accepts that risk when granting. The 0002 request-ID slots use a fixed amount of shared memory per backend slot, so an unprivileged user cannot make them grow. Not checked without the code: whether a grantee can overwrite or reuse another caller's request slot in 0002, and whether custom-plan constants or RLS quals in the logged plan go beyond what log_statement settings allow.

The core node-wrapping design has a qualified owner. Robert Haas reviewed it repeatedly and accepted it, Andres Freund called it acceptable (message #123), and the tree walk now uses planstate_tree_walker (message #190).

No existing way does this job. auto_explain logs a plan only after the query finishes, and the log_before_query idea [P2] was returned without a design. pg_query_state needs a patched core for custom signals (message #146).
